strengths: The paper targets a relevant gap in commonsense evaluation: standard single-answer MCQ benchmarks often hide ambiguity and do not test whether models can compose plausibility judgments across alternatives.
The proposed AND/OR/NEITHER-NOR formulation is simple, easy to evaluate, and potentially useful as a controlled diagnostic for compositional commonsense reasoning.

The experiments cover several model families and prompting regimes, and the reported results reveal a clear and interesting pattern: relatively strong performance on conjunctive/disjunctive cases but sharp failure on negation-based cases.
The paper includes useful supplementary details on prompting, training settings, additional results, and qualitative error patterns.
weaknesses: The dataset construction and validation are not rigorous enough to support the benchmark claims. Most labels are generated and refined by GPT-4o-mini, while human validation covers only a small sample, has only moderate agreement, and reports relatively weak accuracy for NEITHER/NOR, the very category used for the strongest conclusions.

There are internal inconsistencies in the dataset description: Stage 3 is first said to yield 14,997 instances across three relation types, but the final dataset is later said to contain 19,996 instances across four conditions including MIXED. The validation description also mixes atomic-option validation, composed-instance validation, and test-split validation in a confusing way.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate. The paper states that dataset and code are publicly available, but the links are blank. It also claims construction prompts are in Appendix A.3, yet the appendix mainly provides evaluation prompts rather than the GPT-4o-mini generation/refinement prompts needed to reproduce the data.

The train/dev/test split may suffer from leakage if composed instances derived from the same original CommonsenseQA question are split across partitions. This is especially concerning because fine-tuned results are used to argue that the task is learnable rather than artifact-driven.

The task formulation may create strong artifacts: NEITHER/NOR options invert the usual association between plausible content and correctness, so below-chance LLM performance may reflect instruction-following or option-format biases rather than a clean measurement of commonsense negation reasoning.

The human validation protocol is underspecified. It is unclear how annotator judgments over atomic options translate into correctness for composed options, how many composed labels were directly validated, how adjudication was performed, and whether cultural/contextual ambiguity was systematically controlled.

The comparison to CommonsenseQA is suggestive but not fully controlled. The new benchmark changes answer format, label semantics, option length, and negation structure simultaneously, so the observed drop cannot be attributed solely to compositional commonsense reasoning.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, especially claims about “fundamental reasoning limitations” and CommonsenseQA “substantially overestimating” ability. The evidence supports a diagnostic failure pattern on this constructed dataset, but not yet a broad conclusion about commonsense reasoning ability.

strengths: The paper identifies a real limitation of standard commonsense QA benchmarks: single-label MCQ formats often hide ambiguity and do not test whether models can combine plausibility judgments across multiple alternatives.
The proposed operator-based framing, especially separating AND, OR, and NEITHER/NOR conditions, is a potentially useful diagnostic idea for studying compositional commonsense reasoning.
The paper includes a range of model families and evaluation settings, and the broad empirical pattern that negation-based plausibility judgments are difficult is plausible and relevant to NLP.
weaknesses: The dataset construction is not sufficiently sound. Most labels appear to come from GPT-4o-mini generation/refinement plus deterministic composition, with only a small human validation sample. The reported human agreement is only moderate, and NEITHER/NOR label accuracy is low enough to seriously undermine the central claims about model failure.

There are internal inconsistencies in the dataset description: Stage 3 is said to yield 14,997 instances, while the resulting dataset is later reported as 19,996 instances with an added MIXED setting. The split procedure is also unclear, and it appears possible that composed instances from the same base CommonsenseQA question may leak across train/dev/test, which would inflate fine-tuning results.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper states that dataset and code are publicly available, but the URLs are blank. The appendix provides evaluation prompts but not the exact generation/refinement prompts for the dataset pipeline, nor sufficient details on seeds, sampling, filtering, annotator setup, adjudication, or model inference infrastructure.

The validity of the logical task is questionable. The operators are described as not being strict propositional logic but as plausibility-level constructs, yet the paper interprets poor performance as evidence of logical commonsense reasoning failure. This creates an ambiguity between model reasoning errors, unclear semantics, and noisy labels.

Several examples suggest questionable or underspecified gold labels, especially for NEITHER/NOR. Some “implausible” alternatives are context-dependent rather than clearly false, making it hard to know whether low model scores reflect reasoning failure or disagreement with the authors’ constructed labels.

The experimental evidence is too shallow for the strength of the claims. There is little analysis of artifacts, option-position bias, operator lexical cues, label priors, pairwise atomic-option accuracy, or whether models fail at atomic plausibility versus operator composition.

The comparison to CommonsenseQA is not controlled enough to support the claim that CommonsenseQA substantially overestimates commonsense reasoning. The new benchmark changes answer format, option distribution, language style, and label semantics simultaneously.

The paper needs substantial clarity improvements. Important methodological details are scattered or missing, some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, and the relation between human-validated and non-validated subsets is confusing.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and relevant benchmark direction: evaluating commonsense reasoning over composed plausibility judgments rather than only single atomic answers. This is well aligned with NLP evaluation concerns around ambiguity, multiple plausible answers, and logical consistency.

The task formulation is simple and easy to run because it preserves a multiple-choice format while introducing AND, OR, NEITHER/NOR, and MIXED operator conditions. This makes the benchmark accessible to standard prompted and fine-tuned models.

The empirical results are consistent and informative: strong prompted LLMs retain reasonable performance on AND, degrade on OR/MIXED, and fail badly on NEITHER/NOR, while supervised models can learn the constructed task. The comparison to original CommonsenseQA helps motivate why the new benchmark probes a different capability.

The appendix provides useful operational detail, including prompt templates, model choices, decoding settings, annotation guidelines, and additional per-operator results. The error analysis gives plausible qualitative explanations for the main failure modes.
weaknesses: The dataset construction relies heavily on GPT-4o-mini for candidate generation and refinement, but the paper does not provide enough evidence that the generated labels are robust. Human validation covers only a small sample, inter-annotator agreement is moderate, and NEITHER/NOR label accuracy is only 73.6%, which is concerning because the paper’s strongest claim depends on this operator.

There are internal inconsistencies and ambiguities in the dataset description. Stage 3 is first said to yield 14,997 instances with three relation types, but the final dataset is later 19,996 after adding MIXED. It is also unclear whether train/dev/test splits are strictly by original CommonsenseQA question before composition; instance-level splitting could leak base questions and inflate fine-tuned results.

The NEITHER/NOR formulation is unnatural as a multiple-choice answer option and may partly measure prompt interpretation or option-format confusion rather than commonsense negation. Very low performance below random chance may indicate systematic mismatch between task semantics and model instruction following, not only a fundamental reasoning limitation.

The paper claims public dataset/code availability, but the manuscript text appears to omit the actual links. Reproducibility would also benefit from released generation/refinement prompts, deterministic composition code, random seeds, exact sampled CommonsenseQA IDs, annotator counts/payments/backgrounds, and clearer criteria for converting atomic validation into composed-label accuracy.

The experimental comparison is somewhat uneven: decoder-only LLMs are only prompted, while smaller encoder/encoder-decoder models are fine-tuned. This supports claims about prompted failures but makes architectural conclusions limited. The CoT evaluation is restricted to one model, and no closed-model or stronger recent reasoning model baseline is included.

The contribution is sound enough for Findings, but the broader main-conference case is limited by validation scale, possible construction artifacts, and uncertainty about whether the hardest condition reflects genuine compositional commonsense reasoning rather than dataset/interface effects.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant gap: standard commonsense QA benchmarks often collapse multiple plausible interpretations into a single answer, and the proposed AND/OR/NEITHER framing is a clear way to probe compositional plausibility judgments.

The benchmark formulation is easy to understand and remains compatible with multiple-choice evaluation, which makes it convenient for comparing encoder, encoder-decoder, open LLM, and closed-model systems.

The experiments cover a reasonable range of model families and prompting/fine-tuning regimes, and the reported pattern that negation-based plausibility composition is difficult is plausible and potentially useful.
The paper includes some helpful supporting analyses, including diversity statistics, a decomposition analysis, and qualitative error patterns.
weaknesses: The dataset validity is not yet strong enough for a benchmark paper. Most labels are generated/refined by GPT-4o-mini, while human validation covers only 250 base questions from the test split; there is no comparable validation for the training/development sets or the full released dataset.

The reported composed-label accuracy is only 73.6% for NEITHER/NOR even on the adjudicated subset, which is the central condition driving the paper's main claim. This level of label noise substantially weakens the interpretation of very low model scores as reasoning failure rather than benchmark unreliability.

The split protocol appears potentially flawed: the paper says all 19,996 composed instances are split into train/dev/test, but does not state that splits are grouped by original CommonsenseQA question. If compositions derived from the same base question and atomic options appear across splits, fine-tuned results and decomposition conclusions may be inflated by leakage.

The construction rules for answer options are underspecified. The paper says deterministic symbolic composition is used, but does not precisely define how the four candidate composite options are generated, how distractors are sampled, how option balance is controlled, or whether artifacts such as operator tokens, plausible-clause counts, or answer-position biases can solve the task.
The human evaluation of end-task solvability is extremely small, with only 10 examples per condition, so it cannot substantiate claims about human performance or benchmark reliability.

The central comparison to CommonsenseQA is not fully controlled: lower performance may reflect longer composite options, unfamiliar operator wording, generated distractor artifacts, or negation handling, rather than a clean measure of 'commonsense reasoning' beyond the original benchmark.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: dataset/code links appear as empty footnotes, generation prompts are included but decoding/settings for data generation, random seeds, exact sampling, adjudication details, and API/versioning are not sufficiently specified.

The paper would benefit from stronger baselines and controls, such as simple symbolic baselines using independently predicted atomic plausibility, artifact-only classifiers, shuffled/operator-ablated variants, grouped-split evaluation, and larger human validation of composed instances.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant gap: standard commonsense QA benchmarks often collapse multiple plausible interpretations into a single-answer format, and evaluating composed plausibility judgments is a reasonable NLP contribution if the benchmark is sound.

The manuscript includes a reasonably broad model suite, covering prompted open-weight LLMs, proprietary models, encoder/encoder-decoder baselines, and supervised fine-tuning, with additional decomposition and error analyses.
The authors make some effort toward validation, including annotator agreement for atomic options and reporting separate results on a human-validated subset.
weaknesses: The core benchmark validity is insufficiently established. The operators are explicitly not formal logical operators, but the paper still treats AND/OR/NEITHER as if they produce determinate labels. Many provided examples suggest multiple answer choices could satisfy the stated OR or plausibility semantics, making the MCQ gold labels questionable.

Human validation is too limited and indirect. Only 250 source questions, corresponding to half of the test set, are validated, and validation is primarily at the atomic-option level. The composed NEITHER/NOR label accuracy is only 73.6%, implying substantial label noise exactly where the paper's strongest claims are made.

The small human evaluation is inadequate for the claim that the benchmark is human-solvable: it uses only 10 examples per condition, with human accuracy only 0.70 on OR and NEITHER/NOR. This does not convincingly distinguish model failure from ambiguous or noisy items.

The dataset construction is heavily dependent on GPT-4o-mini for generating and refining both plausible and implausible options. The diversity analysis does not address semantic correctness, artifact leakage, or whether generated distractors create exploitable patterns.

The experimental split procedure is unclear and potentially problematic. The paper says the 19,996 composed instances are split into train/dev/test, but if compositions from the same original CommonsenseQA question can appear across splits, supervised fine-tuning results may reflect memorization of source questions or atomic option labels rather than compositional reasoning.

The large performance gap between prompted and fine-tuned models is interpreted as showing inference-time reasoning limitations, but it could also indicate dataset-specific regularities or train/test contamination at the source-question level. The paper does not provide controls to rule this out.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: dataset/code footnotes appear blank in the extracted text, and several important implementation details are underspecified, including exact symbolic composition rules, sampling of answer choices, adjudication procedure, and whether source-question grouping was enforced.

The comparison to CommonsenseQA overstates the conclusion that existing benchmarks overestimate commonsense reasoning. A drop on a noisier, more ambiguous generated benchmark does not by itself demonstrate a true reasoning deficiency.

strengths: Introduces a clear and useful reframing of commonsense QA from single-answer selection to compositional plausibility judgments over pairs of candidate statements, targeting a real limitation of existing benchmarks.

Dataset construction is reasonably well specified: the paper describes the generation, refinement, symbolic composition, annotation guidelines, splits, prompts, and training/evaluation settings, which supports reproducibility if the released code/data match the description.

The empirical evaluation is broad enough to be informative, covering encoder, encoder-decoder, open-weight decoder-only, and proprietary models across zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and fine-tuned settings.

The central empirical pattern is consistent across model families: models perform substantially worse on NEITHER/NOR and mixed compositional settings than on simpler conjunction/disjunction, and fine-tuning shows the task is learnable rather than arbitrary.

The decomposition analysis is a useful addition because it probes whether failures come from atomic plausibility estimation, operator grounding, or multiple-choice distractor competition, rather than only reporting benchmark scores.
weaknesses: The benchmark depends heavily on GPT-4o-mini generated and refined options, while human validation covers only half of the test questions and apparently not the training/development data; this leaves substantial uncertainty about label quality and possible generation artifacts.

The reported composed-label accuracy is notably weak for NEITHER/NOR at 73.6%, precisely the condition supporting the paper’s strongest claim. This does not invalidate the observed model collapse, but it makes the magnitude and interpretation of the failure less secure.

The human solvability evidence is too small: 10 examples per condition is insufficient to establish robust human performance or to calibrate task difficulty, especially for OR and NEITHER/NOR where human accuracy is only 70%.

The logical operators are plausibility-level constructs rather than formal semantics, which is reasonable, but the paper could more carefully separate failures of logical reasoning from failures induced by unnatural answer wording or pragmatic ambiguity in paired options.

The contribution is valuable as a benchmark paper, but the novelty is moderate: it mainly composes existing CommonsenseQA-style items with simple operators. Stronger validation, artifact analysis, and comparison to alternative multi-answer/ambiguous QA formulations would be needed for a clearer main-conference recommendation.
